items.title: Show HN: Verfy – checks an AI coding agent's tool calls before they run
items.story_key: story|title:verfy checks an ai coding agent s tool calls before they run
items.content_excerpt: Verfy CLI (MIT): lock MCP tool definitions and block tools that change after you approved them, guard every Claude Code tool call, signed receipts. pip install verfy The server changes the tool's description after you approved it. Verfy notices the new SHA-256 and blocks the call. Try it on the website . python fix.py looks harmless as a command. Verfy reads the script before it runs and names the line that would wipe the home folder. ▶ The 60-second version (MP4, 1.1 MB): pin the tools, the server ships an update, verfy lock check fails, the gateway hides the tool and denies the call. Recorded with verfy 0.17.0: every terminal line is real output of its demo server ( python -m verfy.demo_server --rugpull ). Stop what your agent shouldn't do. Prove what it did. For Claude Code, Codex, Gemini CLI, Cursor, GitHub Copilot and Devin: Verfy checks each tool call before it runs, stops a tool that changes in secret, and signs a receipt for every call it checks. Where to go: bugs and questions in issues ; security reports privately, as SECURITY.md describes. The Verfy CLI is MIT and always will be. Verfy Cloud is a paid hosted service (free for now; paid plans are not on sale yet). This repository is the CLI; the hosted service is developed separately. Verfy checks every tool call a coding agent makes against your policy before it runs, locks the MCP tool definitions the agent may use, and writes an Ed25519-signed, hash-chained receipt for every call it checks. Verfy Cloud, the hosted service, gives an organization one policy, tool-change approvals, device management, an audit log and evidence exports that anyone can verify offline. Scanners judge a tool when you scan it. Verfy is built for what happens after: the tool changes, the agent calls it, and someone later asks what ran. Use both. From each project's own README, checked 2026-11-05 at the versions listed on the page ( full table and sources ): They also do things Verfy does not: Snyk scans agent skills, Cisco reads server source code and scans packages and binaries, and context-protector can run a guardrail model over tool responses. Without Python, an install script downloads a standalone build. Download it, read it, then run it (there is no curl … | sh one-liner on purpose: Verfy itself asks about that pattern, rule VFY-SH-005): The plugin installs the same hook for every session, plus a skill that lets Claude check your locks for you (approving changes stays with you). items.title: My AI coding agents spend most of their time waiting
items.story_key: story|title:my ai coding agents spend most of their time waiting
items.content_excerpt: I timed every second of an overnight run where my Claude Code agents built features for Note to Self , my iOS app for texting yourself notes. One Claude Code session is the manager. It doesn’t write code. For each feature it starts a fresh agent and takes it through the same steps: The analysis agent got every transcript from the night: the 11 feature agents, the 11 Opus reviews, the 11 Codex logs, the manager’s own session and the git log. It split the night into phases from the manager’s transcript (plan, build, review, fixes), and then put every second of each phase into one bucket: It expects about 10% of the time to land in the wrong bucket at the edges, mostly between UI tests and simulator checks. Their total barely moves. Two thirds of the night was the simulator. The model is fast. Proving the work is slow. The last feature’s fix round was still running when the analysis started, so its bar stops early. The reviews were worth it. They raised 127 findings, and about 36 of them were real bugs. What they cost is the proof that has to run again after every fix. The first of the 11 features was the UI test suite itself. 45 tests became 12 user journeys, each launching the app once and starting from seeded data instead of typing its own. The suite went from 875 seconds to 375, all green. And UI tests still took a third of the night. A suite that takes 57% less time helps less than you’d think when it runs 20 times a night, on top of 191 runs of single classes. The analysis estimates that two features at a time roughly doubles how many fit in a night, and that the other changes cut 30 to 40 minutes off an average 80-minute feature. Next overnight run? Twice as many features done. I’ll measure it the same way. Read my Claude Code transcripts in ~/.claude/projects from the last 3 days. Use the tool call timestamps to split the wall-clock time into model, builds, tests, checks and waiting. Show a table. If your agents build, run tests or drive a browser, I bet the model isn’t your biggest slice.

items.title: Show HN: An agent skill that optimizes code with falsifiable hypotheses
items.story_key: story|title:an agent skill that optimizes code with falsifiable hypotheses
items.content_excerpt: Agents that optimize your code like an algorithm engineer: a falsifiable hypothesis before every experiment, correctness checked after every change, one reviewable patch per accepted change, and a PDF report of the whole session. A skill for Claude Code and Codex, from the Algorithm Engineering Group at Heidelberg University. Algorithm Engineering is a cycle of design, analysis, implementation and experiment, driven by falsifiable hypotheses. AAE hands this cycle to an autonomous agent. During setup you agree with the agent on the benchmark, the metric, the correctness assertions and the budget; then it runs on its own. A falsifiable hypothesis: "changing X will improve the metric by roughly Z, because ..." Predict direction and size of the effect before measuring, from profiling and analysis. Run the benchmark; keep the change only if it is better and still correct, otherwise revert. From the report of the KaHIP kaffpa session: 122 experiments, 69 hypotheses, 41 patches, 3.9x faster in total. In Codex, install the skill with scripts/install_codex_skill.py and call it with $aae ; any other agent can follow AAE.md . To try it first, run the 10-minute quick-start example : a slow but correct shortest-path program with a benchmark and a correctness check. Sessions share what they learned: the knowledge base collects optimization techniques and experiment results, and agents read it before they start. Contributions from your own sessions are welcome. David A. Bader, Adil Chhabra, Ernestine Großmann, Monika Henzinger, Alexander Noe, and Christian Schulz. Agentic Algorithm Engineering: Improving Shared-Memory Exact Minimum Cuts. In 13th DIMACS Implementation Challenge Workshop: Network Flows 2.0, OASIcs, 2027. To appear. Preprint: arXiv:2609.07204 .

items.title: Skip the DRAM Tier: MoRI UMBP Runs the Agentic KV Cache on NVMe
items.summary: On AMD Instinct™ MI355X GPUs, a MoRI UMBP KV pool on NVMe matched a DRAM pool of the same size within 1% for Kimi-K3 on vLLM, and drives that hold a day of agent KV cost less than DRAM that holds 31 minutes.
items.story_key: story|title:skip the dram tier mori umbp runs the agentic kv cache on nvme
items.content_excerpt: Most of the traffic in agentic serving is multi-turn sessions that resend long prefixes. In the AgentX benchmark replaying real Claude Code sessions, the median turn is 142K input tokens, and over 96% of those tokens are a prefix the server has already seen [3] . A KV cache hit means the prefill node only has to process the small delta. A miss forces a full recomputation of the prefix, which burns GPU time and delays the first token. In our 42 runs of Kimi-K3 on vLLM, raising the KV cache hit rate by 1% of prompt tokens, for example from 95% to 96%, was worth about 10% more throughput (Figure 3). A KV cache hit needs the session’s prefix to still be in memory when its next turn arrives. With dozens of sessions open at once, memory runs out. GPU memory goes first, and host DRAM is the usual next tier. But DRAM fills too: Kimi-K3 wrote 2.3 to 4.6 TB of KV to the pool an hour in our runs, so a 1.8 TB DRAM pool, which lists at about $76,000, holds only the last 23 to 47 minutes of it. That led us to a simple question: why not skip the DRAM tier and put vLLM’s KV pool straight on NVMe? We tried it on AMD Instinct™ MI355X GPUs with UMBP, the KV cache pool in AMD’s open-source MoRI library. At the same size, NVMe matched DRAM’s throughput within 1% on Kimi-K3, in two sets of runs on different machines (Figure 1). On a second workload with longer prompts, NVMe came within 1% of a DRAM pool of the same size. The NVMe pool has no DRAM tier: DRAM only buffers new KV on its way to the drives and stages reads, about 80 GB against the DRAM pool’s 1.8 TB. And NVMe’s cost follows the KV it writes, not the KV it holds, so drives rated for Kimi-K3’s writes cost less than that DRAM pool and hold a full day of KV. “Agentic workloads keep sessions open for minutes or hours, and their KV cache quickly outgrows GPU memory and host DRAM. Results like these, with NVMe keeping up with DRAM at the same pool size, change how we think about sizing KV cache capacity in AI clusters. We’re glad to see this work done in the open, in vLLM and MoRI.” — Dennis Kennetz, Principal Infrastructure Engineer, Oracle Cloud Infrastructure DeepSeek already keeps agent KV caches on SSD: the deployment notes for its DeepInfer engine describe three days of retention for agent traffic, on about 14.4 TB of SSD per GPU [4] . This work references DeepInfer for the idea of keeping the KV cache on SSD and for two of its techniques, layer-wise loading and bounded replay, which we test on vLLM below. Figure 1.

items.title: How to build and maintain an agentic evaluation
items.story_key: story|title:how to build and maintain an agentic evaluation
items.content_excerpt: AI evaluations help shape which systems people build, adopt, and trust. An evaluation gives a system tasks, checks its answers or actions, and produces a score. Building and maintaining a useful evaluation therefore takes real work: defining tasks that reflect domain expertise, scoring them reliably, and checking that the results support the claims made. When methods, code, and data stay private, that work is harder for others to scrutinize or build on. Open source offers a means to build stronger, more frequently updated, and more comparable evaluations and the infrastructure around them. Existing tasks, environments, and tools give builders a starting point, so their effort can go to domain expertise and validation. Sharing how an evaluation was built, including what went wrong, lets others find errors, improve it, and reuse it. The Hugging Face hub is the home for AI evaluation: we host around 3500 eval leaderboards and have seen about a 16X growth in eval datasets on the hub in the past year , to about 17000 datasets. In recent months, we have also incorporated support for agentic abstractions that are relevant to evaluation. For example, Traces that store an agent’s work in an easily reviewable and sharable way; Benchmarks that highlight datasets used to evaluate models with leaderboards; and Environments that show datasets used as agentic RL or evaluation environments. In the research community, AI evaluation terminology is notoriously inconsistent . The glossary at the end defines each term we use and notes the other names you may come across. AI evaluation design has evolved in three forms as language models have become more capable and able to perform more complex work: question answer, agentic, and teams or swarms. Question-answer benchmarks such as MMLU (2020) and GPQA (2023) measure knowledge and reasoning through the answers models produce. As models became capable of planning and using tools, agentic benchmarks such as SWE-bench and WebArena expanded the scope to resolving software issues and completing tasks on websites. These tasks require evaluation setups that account for the environment in which the system operates and the changes it makes. Lately, research on multi-agent systems has started to add another dimension: how agents coordinate and what they accomplish together. items.title: Learning When to Ask: Advisor-Aware Post-Training for SLM Agents
items.summary: Small language models (SLMs) are increasingly attractive for cheap, high-throughput agentic deployment, but they remain weak at multi-step reasoning and tool use that long-horizon tasks demand. We study how to post-train an SLM to seek advice from a stronger model and act on that advice itself, following an advisor-executor pattern. Out of the box, this pattern fails across open- and closed-source small-model families: wiring an SLM to an advisor is a harness-design matter that is not enough on its own. A post-training recipe is needed to teach the model when to ask, in a cost-aware fashion, and how to follow advice across steps. Our method, ADAPT (ADvisor-Aware Post-Training), is a multi-stage recipe that instills this behavior, learning entirely from the policy's own rollouts supervised by the environment's outcome, with no learned reward model or human annotation. Across three domains, compared to an untrained harness baseline, ADAPT improves success rate in embodied text reasoning (TextWorld) from 24.5% to 77.3%, code generation (LiveCodeBench) from 21.8% to 56.0%, and deep web search (GAIA) from 17.5% to 49.3%, while querying the advisor sparingly (~1.0-2.1 calls per task). On the two long-horizon domains it closes 70-85% of the gap to an oracle that perfectly times when to ask for advice, and on code generation it exceeds that oracle. The gains persist when the advisor is replaced by one unseen in training, showing that the learned help-seeking policy is robust to a changing advisor rather than tied to the one it was trained with.

items.title: What Helps Language-Model Agents Review Violent Video? A Controlled Comparison with a Human Evidence Reference
items.summary: Systems that flag violent video for a human operator can now be built from language models without training, by combining perception models and letting a language model decide. We ask how the observations of the perception models should reach the decision, and which evidence matters. On the XD-Violence test set (799 clips) we fix one set of perception agents (video description, object detection, sound tagging, speech recognition and speech tagging) and one reasoning model, and compare three interfaces: messages between agents, a typed evidence graph explored with tools, and flat text read in one pass; and a single audio-visual model given the raw clip. Two annotators provide a human reference that records the decision, the incident segments and whether they relied on sight, sound or speech. Flat text matches the single model (F1 0.967 against 0.968), while the graph agent and message passing are less accurate; a variant of the graph agent developed on a separate set did not close the gap, and both graph summaries and multi-turn tool use lowered accuracy. These results hold with reworded prompts and with a larger reasoning model, except that the larger model weakens message passing enough for the graph agent to beat it. Sound events improve F1 by +0.012 [+0.004, +0.021], in line with the annotators, who used sound or speech on most violent clips. Citations of stored observations are faithful, changing about half of the decisions when removed, but no more so with the graph than with flat text, and the agent pipeline costs about 3 times the GPU time of the single model. We also report two artefacts of vision-language describers that mislead pipelines built on them.

items.title: How to build a knowledge factory for AI agents
items.summary: The knowledge factory is how LangChain keeps its agents' company knowledge current: agents flag what's missing, and a curator agent fixes it in the background.
items.story_key: story|title:how to build a knowledge factory for ai agents
items.content_excerpt: In order to make AI work for your company, the missing bit is not better models, it’s not just more context - it’s better knowledge. It’s knowledge of how your company works, what standards for operating you have in place, where data is stored and how it’s accessed. Your most efficient employees have this knowledge in their head. They know who to talk to, where to go to answer questions, why you do things in a particular way. That knowledge is often tacit, implicit, scattered - sometimes present only in their head, sometimes scattered across a variety of documents. In order to make AI work for your company, you need to collect, curate, and maintain a representation of that knowledge to pass to agents. The system that helps you do that is what we’re calling a knowledge factory. We’ve built this at LangChain in a few ways. Our internal GTM and content studio agents are powered by a knowledge factory. LangSmith Engine (our agent that runs over traces and suggests fixes) maintains a knowledge factory per agent as well. This blog shares our learnings. Knowledge is the reusable understanding we maintain so it can do that task correctly: what a metric means, which source to trust, or how we handle a particular situation. Sometimes written down, often not. A knowledge factory turns scattered documents and experience into knowledge that can become context for future work. So knowledge is a form of context that the agent will get, but it’s often not (and shouldn’t be) the only context the agent gets. Other types of context you already ingest/store reliably, and that can just be provided directly to the agent (see the section on quickly changing data below). The idea of software factories has risen sharply over the past year and a half. The idea is that rather than having your best engineers actually build software, they should build the factory (the systems) to help everyone at the company build software more efficiently. The actual building of the software can be done by agents. General knowledge work is now following a similar path. Agents are good enough to make presentations, launch videos, do outbound. You should be leveraging them as much as possible for those tasks. But in order for them to accomplish those tasks they need all that tacit, implicit, scattered knowledge. items.title: Ranking-Preserving Coreset Selection for Efficient Evolutionary Hyperparameter Optimization
items.summary: Hyperparameter optimization (HPO) is essential for high predictive performance, but its computational cost becomes prohibitive when candidate configurations require repeated training on large datasets. This paper proposes a ranking-preserving coreset (RPC) selection framework for accelerating evolutionary HPO. The method constructs a compact coreset that preserves the relative ranking of hyperparameter configurations observed on the full training data. Coreset selection is formulated as an evolutionary optimization problem that maximizes Spearman rank correlation between full-data and subset-based configuration rankings while penalizing subset size. The selected coreset is then used for HPO with three evolutionary algorithms: Genetic Algorithm (GA), Cross-generational elitist Selection, Heterogeneous Recombination and Cataclysmic Mutation (CHC), and Particle Swarm Optimization (PSO). Experiments on seven tabular, two text, and two image benchmark datasets show that RPC substantially reduces HPO time while maintaining test accuracy comparable to full-dataset HPO across decision tree, text classification, and image classification tasks. Across datasets and optimizers, HPO-stage speedups range from approximately 1.14x to 8.80x, while the one-time coreset construction cost is accounted for separately through end-to-end runtime and break-even analysis. On 20 held-out configurations excluded from coreset construction, RPC achieves higher ranking correlation than same-size random sampling on 8 of 11 datasets (dataset-level Wilcoxon signed-rank test, p = 0.014). These results show that ranking preservation extends beyond the configurations used during selection. The one-time construction cost can be amortized when the coreset is reused across HPO runs.

items.title: claude-code v2.1.326
items.summary:
What's changed

  • Added support for turning on Code Mode while agent teams are enabled; if you already turned it on, sessions with teams on now start in Code Mode
  • Added a startup warning when an --allowedTools, --disallowedTools or --tools value has an entry that doesn't look like a complete rule
  • Added a message explaining why MCP servers stop loading when an administrator adds managed-mcp.json during a session
  • Added a row to /status that says when your provider or an environment variable such as DISABLE_TELEMETRY turns features off
  • Added a note in /plugin and claude plugin list when a malformed plugin.json field such as author or homepage is ignored
  • Added Ctrl+O to show hidden startup notices
  • Added a hint in the empty prompt that says what to do after a request fails
  • Added an esc to stop footer hint in a subagent's view where Esc would stop it
  • Added OTEL_RESOURCE_INCLUDE_HOST to include host.name and host.id in OpenTelemetry resource attributes (off by default)
  • Added overflowX="scroll" on a mod's Box, and maxLines and wrap="clip" on its Text
  • Fixed cp of a file being refused when only its source was covered by an Edit deny rule
  • Fixed Bash commands that delete or overwrite files (find -delete, cat a > b, sort -o) being summed up in the transcript as a search or a read
  • Fixed a misleading "Dangerous rm operation" warning in the Bash permission prompt on some commands with no rm that Claude Code can't read reliably
  • Fixed background sessions losing the LLM gateway your shell exported after a crash, after a reopen from another folder, or when the background service lacks it: they now stop before any model request
  • Fixed the background service ending your own processes, such as an SSH login, when a process number on its list had been reused by another user's process
  • Fixed rules added in /permissions or at a main-conversation tool prompt, and /add-dir folders, looking saved when the settings file couldn't be written; the terminal now warns and names it
  • Fixed a failed MCP headersHelper, or one not run in an untrusted folder, making other sessions start without that server, for most servers with no stored OAuth refresh token
  • Fixed managed settings with certain key names stopping Claude Code from starting or affecting other managed files
  • Fixed settings files with values nested thousands of levels deep crashing Claude Code or applying only some of the time; values past 64 levels are now dropped with a warning
  • Fixed a settings file saved with an error mid-session being skipped silently; a warning now names the file
  • Fixed the subagent model set in managed settings not applying in Claude Desktop's Code tab; it now overrides your own, as in a terminal, unless those settings also pick a provider or gateway
  • Fixed sandboxed commands failing to start on Linux when the home or config directory is reached through a symlink into /net and sandbox settings deny reads of it
  • Fixed empty placeholder files, including .git/config.lock, sometimes being left in the project on Linux when Claude Code was stopped during a sandboxed command
  • Fixed Up then Enter answering Yes at the folder trust prompt shown under an already trusted parent folder
  • Fixed an extra Enter at the end of setup accepting the offer to make auto mode the default
  • Fixed a message typed over the startup auto mode offer being lost, and its Enter accepting the offer
  • Fixed a note typed on a permission prompt being sent to Claude after Tab had hidden it
  • Fixed PreToolUse hooks in managed settings leaving no OpenTelemetry tool_decision event or permission_denials entry when they refused a direct tool call
  • Fixed letters typed over /sandbox or a delete question in /permissions moving the selection
  • Fixed resumed sessions losing recent turns after a crash when the previous turn ended with an empty reply
  • Fixed resumed sessions losing earlier conversation history when Claude Code ran low on memory
  • Fixed a re-sent file overwriting Claude's changed copy in Remote Control and cloud sessions on Linux with no feature flags loaded: the copy moves to a .kept- folder, or the new file isn't saved
  • Fixed a background session being killed and its request lost when you opened, stopped or removed the older session whose conversation it had resumed
  • Fixed claude purge hiding its prompts when stdout is redirected, where one unseen Enter could delete a project's data; they now show on the terminal
  • Fixed the spend limit menu removing the monthly limit without asking when Backspace and Enter were pressed as it opened
  • Fixed /rewind restoring only some files after running /branch twice while a slow backup copy was still running
  • Fixed /rewind saying "No code changes" when a shell command changed files it can't restore; a turn whose changes weren't tracked now reads "Code changes unknown"
  • Fixed /rewind: Esc now cancels its summary, its list shows more than one past prompt in fullscreen, and a long prompt no longer hides its warning about losing later file changes
  • Fixed Ctrl+C or Ctrl+D twice in /skills quitting Claude Code and dropping changes; it now saves and closes the panel
  • Fixed the usage limit menu erasing your draft and opening while you were typing
  • Fixed pasted text and images being dropped when ↑ recalls a draft cleared with Esc Esc
  • Fixed an edited typed answer to Claude's question sending the old text when you moved on without pressing Enter
  • Fixed going back to a question you answered from its list putting the cursor on the first option, where Enter replaced your answer
  • Fixed /feedback and /bug sending the report when you typed a space on the confirmation screen, and losing the typed report after Ctrl+O or Ctrl+Z
  • Fixed a prompt typed after --add-dir, --allowedTools or another list option being dropped without a message
  • Fixed /plan <description> ignoring the description when plan mode was already on
  • Fixed valid PDFs being dropped from the conversation after the API rejected a different PDF read in the same batch
  • Fixed a session ending after a single failed memory allocation while drawing the screen
  • Fixed compaction on Bedrock, Vertex and Foundry, and with telemetry turned off, sometimes replying to one of your messages instead of summarizing, or leaving Claude's last reply out of the summary
  • Fixed image-heavy sessions on Vertex AI getting stuck on a 400 error about the request size exceeding a 30 MB limit, instead of compacting and retrying

  • Fixed grep in the Bash tool silently skipping some text files

  • Changed automatic compaction in plan mode to use the model answering you, such as Opus with opusplan, so it can cost more
  • Changed Cowork cloud sessions to hold an organization's OpenTelemetry export until the first turn; a session that gets no message now sends nothing, so claude_code.session.count can fall
  • Changed Claude's messages to a session on another machine to be refused when your session uses an API key, auth token, profile or workload identity beside a saved claude.ai login
  • Changed --bare sessions on an unapproved API key: moving one to the background is now refused in most setups, and claude --bare --bg exits with an error if the background service lacks the key
  • Changed "Continue automatically at usage limit" to stop with a notice, sending nothing, when your login changes or ends during the wait
  • Remote Control: Changed how it connects through a proxy: requests now use a CONNECT tunnel, so a proxy that refuses CONNECT stops Remote Control with an error
  • Remote Control: Changed the session debug logs written under --verbose to go to ~/.claude/child-logs/
  • Self-hosted runner: Changed Linux and macOS sessions with no gh to get a built-in gh api by default, via Anthropic, which adds their GitHub sign-in, if any; --use-anthropic-gh false turns it off
  • Changed agent view so that quitting with Ctrl+C twice, Ctrl+D twice or /exit after pressing ← in an empty conversation ends that session, instead of leaving it running for 5 minutes
  • Changed --await-initialize to be refused with --bg or --worktree --tmux, which never read the initialize request, instead of starting without the fields it carries
  • Changed worktree creation, /teleport and IDE checkouts to run git with a stricter PATH; a git filter or helper may need its full path
  • Changed the card for approving a subagent's plan to two choices, "Yes, and switch to default (ask each time) for this session" and "No", chosen with the arrow keys and Enter (typed text moves to No)
  • Changed the /claude-api skill to build agents on Managed Agents by default, unless you want to host the agent loop yourself
  • Changed /usage in fullscreen mode to show plan limit bars before session cost for subscribers; /cost still starts with cost
  • Changed the wording of some messages that claude subcommands print; JSON output is unchanged
  • Changed first-run setup to preselect the "Auto (match terminal)" theme instead of Dark mode
  • Changed fullscreen /cd to refuse "Yes" while its trust prompt doesn't fit, with a line saying to make the window taller
  • Removed the tmux notice that said the mouse wheel needs set -g mouse on in fullscreen; the wheel scrolls without it
  • Removed the spinner tip that suggested /clear 30 minutes into a running turn
  • [VSCode] Added a claudeCode.promptSuggestions setting that turns prompt suggestions off
  • [VSCode] Fixed "Rewind code to here" in a forked conversation sometimes undoing one turn too many and deleting files created in that turn
  • [VSCode] Fixed the Sandbox dialog creating empty files and folders in the home directory and the project's .git folder while the sandbox is off
  • [VSCode] Fixed the saved sign-in being lost on some networks
  • [VSCode] Fixed sign-in ending when a verification code, a web address or a code from another sign-in attempt is pasted; the panel now says what to paste instead
  • [VSCode] Fixed the sign-in screen showing briefly each time a panel or window opened while signed in to Console without an API key
  • [VSCode] Fixed the usage-limit banner's "Request more" button for Team and Enterprise members coming back after each press without sending anything, after you signed in again during a session
  • [VSCode] Fixed /ide in a second Claude Code session silently losing the editor connection back to the first session; the newest connection now wins and the displaced session shows how to switch back
  • [VSCode] Fixed saved memories not being listed in the Memory dialog, or RAM use growing without end, when the memory folder held symlink loops, and a hang when it held a named pipe
  • [VSCode] Fixed a running command's live output stopping after one failed read
  • [VSCode] Fixed "Open in Terminal" showing only the shell's error when claude could not be started: in bash, zsh, fish and Git Bash, a notice now explains why and links to the install guide
  • [VSCode] Fixed the panel showing no "Open artifact" link after Claude publishes an artifact
  • [VSCode] Fixed the prompt suggestion hiding the "attach selected text" hint while the chat panel is unfocused
  • [VSCode] Fixed buttons with no visible border in the high-contrast themes, and the dark welcome art on the sign-in screen in Light High Contrast
  • [VSCode] Improved Edit and Write speed: no wait for new problems on files that are not open in a tab when the editor has been reporting none for such files
  • [VSCode] Changed a running command's live output in the chat to look like the command card's OUT row
  • [VSCode] Changed the text of extension errors in event listeners, views and activation to stay out of the editor's own error telemetry

items.title: Release 2.75.0 corresponding to NGC container 26.11
items.summary:
Triton Inference Server

The Triton Inference Server provides a cloud inferencing solution optimized for both CPUs and GPUs. The server provides an inference service via an HTTP or GRPC endpoint, allowing remote clients to request inferencing for any model being managed by the server. For edge deployments, Triton Server is also available as a shared library with an API that allows the full functionality of the server to be included directly in an application.

New Features and Improvements

  • PyTorch backend: Added AOTI BF16 input/output support.
  • THIRD-PARTY-NOTICES.txt is now included in the containers.
  • Fixed a use-after-free in the dynamic batcher and a preserve_ordering completion-slot issue on response-cache hits.
  • Prevented silent gRPC stream cancellations under backpressure.
  • Bounded the decompressed HTTP inference response size in the client library.
  • Perf Analyzer: Honored supplied output shapes, propagated the binary exit code, tagged the wheel as platform-specific, and limited profile-data export to the needed inputs and outputs.
  • Python backend: Now logs when the backend stub exits on a crash signal.

Known Issues

  • The Triton TensorRT-LLM Backend container image is not included in this release.
  • vLLM's v0 API and Ray are affected by vulnerabilities. Users should consider their own architecture and mitigation steps which may include but should not be limited to:
    • Do not expose Ray executors and vLLM hosts to a network where any untrusted connections might reach the host.
    • Ensure that only the other vLLM hosts are able to connect to the TCP port used for the XPUB socket. Note that the port used is random.
  • When using Valgrind or other leak detection tools on AGX-Thor or DGX-Spark systems, you might see memory leaks attributed to NvRmGpuLibOpen.
  • Valgrind or other memory leak detection tools may occasionally report leaks related to DCGM. These reports are intermittent and often disappear on retry.
  • CuPy has issues with the CUDA 13 Device API in multithreaded contexts. Avoid using tritonclient cuda_shared_memory APIs in multithreaded environments until fixed by CuPy.
  • TensorRT calibration cache may require size adjustment in some cases, which was observed for the IGX platform.
  • The core Python binding may incur an additional D2H and H2D copy if the backend and frontend both specify device memory to be used for response tensors.
  • A segmentation fault related to DCGM and NSCQ may be encountered during server shutdown on NVSwitch systems. A possible workaround for this issue is to disable the collection of GPU metrics tritonserver --allow-gpu-metrics false ....
  • When using TensorRT models, if auto-complete configuration is disabled and is_non_linear_format_io:true for reformat-free tensors is not provided in the model configuration, the model may not load successfully.
  • When using Python models in decoupled mode, users need to ensure that the ResponseSender goes out of scope or is properly cleaned up before unloading the model to guarantee that the unloading process executes correctly.
  • Triton Inference Server with vLLM backend currently does not support running vLLM models with tensor parallelism sizes greater than 1 and the default "distributed_executor_backend" setting when using explicit model control mode. In attempt to load a vllm model (tp > 1) in explicit mode, users could potentially see failure at initialize step: could not acquire lock for <_io.BufferedWriter name='<stdout>'> at interpreter shutdown, possibly due to daemon threads. For the default model control mode, after server shutdown, vllm related sub-processes are not killed. Related vllm issue: vllm-project/vllm#6766. Please specify "distributed_executor_backend":"ray" in the model.json when deploying vllm models with tensor parallelism > 1.
  • When loading models with file override, multiple model configuration files are not supported. Users must provide the model configuration by setting parameter "config" : "<JSON>" instead of custom configuration file in the following format: "file:configs/<model-config-name>.pbtxt" : "<base64-encoded-file-content>".
  • TensorRT-LLM backend provides limited support of Triton extensions and features.
  • The TensorRT-LLM backend may core dump on server shutdown. This impacts server teardown only and will not impact inferencing.
  • The Java CAPI is known to have intermittent segfaults.
  • Some systems which implement malloc() may not release memory back to the operating system right away causing a false memory leak. This can be mitigated by using a different malloc implementation. Tcmalloc and jemalloc are installed in the Triton container and can be used by specifying the library in LD_PRELOAD. NVIDIA recommends experimenting with both tcmalloc and jemalloc to determine which one works better for your use case.
  • Auto-complete may cause an increase in server start time. To avoid a start time increase, users can provide the full model configuration and launch the server with --disable-auto-complete-config.
  • Auto-complete does not support PyTorch models due to lack of metadata in the model. It can only verify that the number of inputs and the input names matches what is specified in the model configuration. There is no model metadata about the number of outputs and datatypes. Related PyTorch bug: pytorch/pytorch#38273
  • Triton Client PIP wheels for ARM SBSA are not available from PyPI and pip will install an incorrect Jetson version of Triton Client library for Arm SBSA. The correct client wheel file can be pulled directly from the Arm SBSA SDK image and manually installed.
  • Traced models in PyTorch seem to create overflows when int8 tensor values are transformed to int32 on the GPU. Refer to pytorch/pytorch#66930 for more information.
  • Triton cannot retrieve GPU metrics with MIG-enabled GPU devices.
  • Triton metrics might not work if the host machine is running a separate DCGM agent on bare-metal or in a container.

Client Libraries and Examples

The client libraries and examples are available in this release exclusively via the Ubuntu 24.04–based NGC Container. The SDK container includes the client libraries and examples, Performance Analyzer, and Model Analyzer. See Getting the Client Libraries for more information.

ManyLinux Assets (early access)

This release was compiled with AlmaLinux 8.9 based out of manylinux_2_34 and can be used on RHEL 9 and later versions.
See the included README.md for complete details about installation, verification, and support.
This release supports ensembles. Confirm CUDA, TensorRT, ONNX Runtime, PyTorch, and Python versions in the shipped README.md.
Some optional backend features such as the PyTorch backend's TorchTRT extension are not currently supported.
